sections.title: Hinduism
sections.html:
It goes without saying that this chapter makes no claim to cover, even in small part, the Eastern religions with their many branches. The intention is to focus on the fundamental position of Judaism regarding them. In general, the encounter between Jews and the adherents of the Eastern religions was limited, and therefore the Sages of Israel did not deal with them much. Accordingly, we will take a brief look at the Eastern religions in light of the Jewish outlook, which on the one hand looks favourably upon humanity, tries to learn from every culture all the good that can be learned from it, and seeks to benefit every person according to his way; and on the other hand utterly rejects the idolatrous outlook and fights the evil that grows from it. We will begin with the Hindu religion, which is the oldest of the Eastern religions and with which more than a billion people are associated today. From Hinduism grew the Buddhist religion with its various streams, whose believers number more than half a billion people (below, sections 6-7), as well as smaller religions such as Sikhism and Jainism (below, section 8).

The Hindu religion first appeared some three thousand five hundred years ago in northwest India, and from there it spread throughout India. The Indian subcontinent is characterised by the abundance of life that flows through it: plentiful water, abundant crops, lush and varied vegetation, and magnificent landscapes of mountains, valleys, forests, rivers and deserts, in which countless kinds of animals live. For generations, visitors to India have returned awestruck by their encounter with the abundance and richness of its land, its landscapes and its people, and have described with wonder the array of colours, tastes and smells that accompany the lives of people in India. Human society in India is also many-hued: side by side live the exceedingly wealthy, who have built magnificent palaces, and the destitute, who live in the street; sages and men of spirit alongside the ignorant and coarse-hearted; criminals alongside people of kindness; people of sensitivity and compassion toward every living thing alongside exploiters who are indifferent to the suffering of others. What is interesting is that in India these opposites and contradictions exist side by side in a kind of acceptance, and within a complex and many-faceted outlook.

Within this varied and fertile abundance the Hindu religion grew, with a ramified system of idols unlike any other in the world. Light and shadow, good and evil, spirit and matter, are intermingled in it, and give tremendous inspiration for the creation of many religious streams and rites, countless idols and rich stories, accompanied by artistic creation in sculpture, painting, poetry and dance. Thus the Hindu religion, with its many idols and its rites and myths of dazzling imagination, reflects the rich and abundant variety in the nature of the world and in the soul of the individual and of society, and gives the good and evil within them various interpretations from which innumerable insights can be reached. Although it has various kinds of rites for many gods, there were almost no zealous religious wars in India, since the guiding principle of Hinduism is that there is room for all the gods and for every combination of them, and each group may choose for itself the rites that suit it; and even within each group a person may emphasise the idols and rites close to his heart, or be indifferent to all of them.

sections.title: The Evil in Idolatry
sections.html:
One of the foundations of the faith of Israel is that idolatry is falsehood, and that idol worship harms man. This can also be seen by examining its negative influence on society and culture in India.

The basic trait of faith ought to spur a person to endless elevation by adding goodness and blessing to the world, and this through attachment to faith in the One God, for when all the forces in the world are directed toward Him, the good in the world increases and the world is made more perfected. By contrast, avoda zara (idolatry) perpetuates reality as it is, gives it divine justification, and thereby blocks the inner demand for elevation and rectification. For by giving corporeal form to the divine according to all the forces and shades within man and nature, one also gives justification to the bad traits in man and perpetuates them, without striving to correct them. Thus there are good gods and evil gods, and man stands before good and evil without an absolute decision in favour of the good, since the evil gods too must be worshipped and appeased. That is to say, it is clear that the good is good, and one who walks in its path merits enlightenment and tranquillity; but since evil too represents divine forces, it too has a place, and its benefit may even be great, since through it one can attain more wealth, power and pleasures.

As in all idolatrous religions, within Hinduism too there existed in the past rites of licentiousness and prostitution, and at times even human sacrifice to appease the anger of the evil gods. Robbers and murderers, too, had recognised idols, which symbolised violence as a decisive force in reality, and under their patronage they committed their crimes with cruelty. Even the men of the law who fought them did not deny that the criminals were acting in the name of real idols. Rather, the men of the law acted in the name of the central and accepted Hindu stream, which held that the criminals deviated from the true faith by giving positive value to the forces of destruction, whereas the truth is that the forces of destruction are meant to fight evil and not to justify it. These positions, in their various aspects, find expression in the various myths that tell of the quarrels, hatreds and wars between the idols.

In certain streams of Hinduism, the husband was regarded within the family as the image of the god, whom one must serve and obey; and after his death, the praiseworthy act of his widow was that, when his body was burned, she would be burned with him while still alive. Such cases were rare, and the vast majority of widows were not burned, but they lived in great suffering, because they were regarded as women to whom evil and a curse clung. Therefore people avoided maintaining social ties with them, and those who pitied them gave them charity outside the house. Following this tradition, to this day most widows, even young ones, do not remarry.

sections.title: Social Class and Reincarnation
sections.html:
With the support of the religious leaders, a rigid system of four castes (varnas), that is, social classes, developed: 1) Brahmins, the religious leaders; 2) warriors; 3) workers; 4) servants. Below them there is a further class, the impure ("untouchables"), from whom members of the four castes kept their distance, avoiding touching them and avoiding eating and drinking from anything the impure had touched. The most degrading jobs were assigned to the impure, and they lived in shameful poverty. The class of the "impure" numbers about twenty percent of the whole society, and to this day many of them suffer severe discrimination, despite the democratic constitution that has governed India for nearly eighty years, and despite the educational activity of the government, which tries to moderate the attitude toward them.

The idea that underlies the castes is the belief that a person's soul is in a constant process of reincarnation: birth, life and death, and again birth, life and death, over and over. According to his "karma", that is, according to the sum of a person's actions in his previous incarnations, his soul will be reincarnated into its next life cycle. If he corrupted himself with evil deeds, including bad behaviour toward the various gods, he has brought bad karma upon himself, and he will be born into a lower caste, or even into the body of an animal, a plant or an inanimate object. And if he did good deeds and honoured the gods that express the various forces in the world, then his karma is good and he will be born into a family of a higher caste. According to this, a person has no cause to complain about his status, since he was born into his caste according to his deeds in his previous incarnations.

Accordingly, a person's rectification depends on his acceptance of his fate and of the forces of nature and the various gods, including the evil ones, and within this framework he must strive to behave properly. Indeed, there is a large measure of truth in this recognition that a person's fate is dictated from birth, since a person's family, social and genetic background greatly influence his fate, and there is an advantage in a person accepting his fate and not trying to reach a status beyond what he is able to attain. Moreover, in the Hindu outlook a person can also choose to change his status significantly, but this will happen in the next incarnation, by virtue of his acceptance of his fate in the present incarnation and his doing the best he can.

In Judaism, by contrast, on the one hand it is indeed agreed that all that falls to a person's lot at birth is by individual Divine Providence from God; but its purpose is that he should rise and advance in his present life on earth as much as possible. For faith in the infinite God spurs a person to rise ever higher, without end. Therefore, in Judaism even a mamzer (one born of a forbidden union), whose lineage is so blemished that he is forbidden to marry an ordinary Jewish woman, can engage in Torah study and reach a spiritual level higher than a High Priest. Similarly regarding the poor person: although it is a mitzva to do kindness with him and to sustain him with dignity, the aim is to bring him out of the cycle of poverty and set him on his feet. Therefore there is a mitzva upon every community to give all the children of the community, including the poor, a full education in Torah, derekh eretz (proper conduct) and good deeds, so that they will be able to stand on their own feet. Moreover, the Sages taught (Nedarim 81a): "Be careful with the children of the poor, for from them Torah will go forth." For it is precisely lack and hardship that can drive a person to great growth.

sections.title: Developments in the Hindu Religion
sections.html:
Over the thousands of years of the Hindu religion's existence, a process of progress and elevation took place within it, toward belief in a single source and a strengthening of moral values. There are two causes for this:

The first and principal one: the Hindu religion did not stagnate, and alongside the multiplication of idols and the addition of countless interpretations and myths, it deepened its religious and philosophical thought. From a focus on offering sacrifices to the idols, as appears in the ancient writings, the Vedas ("knowledge"), it rose to rites expressing inner intention, which were expounded in the Upanishads. Later, within the stories of the gods and the myths (such as the Bhagavad Gita), foundations that had been hidden in the ancient writings were emphasised, concerning the supreme root called "Brahman", which is infinite and the soul of the entire universe, and even the gods are manifestations of it. In continuation of this, greater emphasis was placed on the moral foundation of choosing the good, which drives the cycle of reincarnation, which expresses the cosmic order to which even the gods are subject.1

Second, this position was strengthened as a result of the encounter with the monotheistic religions. Some twelve hundred years ago the Muslims conquered northern India, and later its centre as well. And some five hundred years ago Christians arrived in India, first merchants from Portugal and afterwards the English. Through them, belief in the One God and moral values originating in the Tanakh (Hebrew Bible) were absorbed into Hindu culture. Over the years many Hindus also visited other countries and encountered the monotheistic religions, and as a result they delved deeper into the Hindu religion and uncovered the unifying foundation within it. The encounter with the Western religions that were influenced by Judaism intensified greatly in the days of British rule, which lasted nearly three hundred years: at first partially, through the "British East India Company", and afterwards through more than a hundred years of direct rule. British rule exploited India shamefully, but it also moderated cruel customs and severe discrimination against the lower classes. Thus, consciously and unconsciously, the values of the Tanakh became fundamental values in Hindu culture, according to which Indian society today strives to build itself.

It is worth noting that the vast richness of the Hindu religion, which includes countless idols, rites and images, as well as the important place given to meditation, which allows deep inner listening, created an especially pluralistic position toward different religions and rites. This enabled it to digest new ideas more easily and to integrate them into itself.2 And when it encountered foundational ideas of the kind that came forth from the Torah of Israel, concerning belief in One God and the moral demand for the rectification of man and society, it was even able to give them a central place, since they echoed deep chords that had existed within it from days of old. This is apparently the reason why, of all the idolatrous religions that collapsed before the truth and light that flowed from the faith of Israel through the monotheistic religions, the Hindu religion survived with vitality, for it has the capacity to absorb lofty ideas and to advance through them.

sections.title: Summary of the Good and the Evil in Hinduism
sections.html:
Since in Hindu worship statues are venerated, offerings are brought before them and incense is burned, for Israel it is considered full-fledged avoda zara, and therefore all the rites performed before the idols are forbidden to Jews by Torah law. And although many Hindus also direct their worship to God, who is the supreme source of all the various forces expressed in the statues, for Israel even avoda zara be-shituf (idolatry in association with God) is considered full-fledged avoda zara. For Israel is obligated to cleave to the pure faith of God's unity, in order to raise the world to the highest level of faith and morality.

For Benei Noaḥ (non-Jews), however, according to many opinions, as long as they believe in God as the source of all forces, there is no prohibition of avoda zara in the Hindu religion (see above 5:10, note 12). And although there is no prohibition in this, the damage caused by the idolatrous corporealisation is great, since despite the great richness of Hindu culture, its idolatrous side gives justification to many injustices. The more Hinduism is purified of the conception that the idols have independent power, and the more belief in the One God and the morality that flows from it is strengthened, the more they will be able, with the help of the beautiful ideas in Hinduism, to act to add blessing to the world. Out of the richness of thought and imagination regarding man and his soul, they will be able to offer humanity an abundance of proposals for personal expression and ways of coping with the hardships of existence. Thereby the pluralism of Hinduism will unite into a movement toward tikkun olam (rectification of the world), and will not scatter, wasting precious energies in vain. And thereby the rich and magnificent art that developed in India, in the fields of literature, poetry, painting, sculpture, architecture, music and the like, will inspire members of all nations to add beauty and delight to the world. They will likewise be able to give the world the special sensitivity they have developed toward all animals and plants, which is based on respect for every creature and the aspiration not to harm it. The more they cleave to belief in the One God and to morality, the more they will direct this sensitivity toward the overall movement for the rectification and redemption of the world.

sections.title: Buddhism
sections.html:
Some thousand years after the appearance of the Hindu religion, the Buddhist religion emerged from it. According to Buddhist tradition, its founder was Siddhartha Gautama, an Indian prince who lived at the foot of the Himalaya mountains (approximately 563-479 BCE). When he left the palace he encountered the suffering that pervades human life and the infinite pain it causes, and from the depths of his soul arose the existential question: how can man be redeemed from this terrible suffering? He left the palace and practised abstinence and self-mortification, studied with Hindu teachers, and found that their teaching, their self-mortifications and the yoga exercises they teach do not bring a fundamental remedy to the problem of suffering. Through prolonged meditation he delved into his consciousness until he attained enlightenment, and for this reason he is called Buddha, "the enlightened one". In his enlightenment he understood that human suffering stems from a person's cravings, and that his salvation lies in ceasing to crave. He should adopt neither asceticism nor hedonism, but walk the middle way, and through meditation exercises silence his cravings for wealth and honour, for food and drink. He should also not lust for sexual gratification nor seek recognition from his fellows, but live his life out of deep, inner tranquillity. And the more he persists in this, the more he will rise to that inner tranquillity and enlightenment called "nirvana", and thereby be redeemed forever.

In contrast to the Hindu religion, which guides its believers to experience life with full intensity and sensuality, and, through the idolatrous outlook, to give meaning to all the different situations, Buddhism strives to extinguish the craving for these experiences and to empty oneself of thoughts and emotions, for from them stems the connection to the external world, and instead to connect to the absolute void, which is also absolute being and light.

In Hinduism a person strives to strengthen the inner self, called "atman", until it merges with the supreme source. This is done by walking the right path and strengthening the inner self through rich and meaningful experiences. On the other hand, since a person need not strive to achieve any particular goal but only to perform the action correctly, all the disasters that befall him will not harm him and need not sadden him; rather, they are his path to strengthening the inner self until it unites with the supreme source. For Buddhism, by contrast, the aim is to nullify the consciousness of the "self", for the very thought of its existence is an illusion that causes suffering, just as all the cravings and suffering of the "self" are an illusion. That is to say, according to Buddhism, the nullification of personality and cravings is not a solution that contradicts the truth; rather, this is the absolute truth: that the egoistic personality and its cravings are an illusion, and consequently, when a person clings to them they cause him suffering, and the more his consciousness is free of egoism, the more it will be free of illusions and he will be able to attain tranquillity and happiness. It follows that the Hindu rites are also superfluous, since their purpose is to strengthen the harmful illusions. The division into castes in the Hindu religion is likewise perceived in the Buddhist religion as a harmful illusion that shackles a person and causes him suffering.

sections.title: The Buddhist Path
sections.html:
Devout Buddhists take upon themselves monastic vows, withdraw from life and devote themselves to the nullification of the self and of cravings, in order to attain enlightenment and tranquillity, until they attain absolute and eternal nirvana. Other people who believe in Buddhism, by contrast, receive from it guidance for proper living, in which a person refrains from adultery, theft and other acts that harm others; refrains from alcohol and drugs; strives to do good deeds and to act with compassion and kindness; and supports the monks, who rise to higher levels and guide the general public.

Through meditation exercises, Buddhist believers strengthen their identification with Buddhist values and loosen their attachment to the various cravings and to the tension that accompanies the desire to satisfy them. They look upon their lives and aspirations favourably, with a deep and detached gaze, and thereby attain stability and tranquillity. When they persist in this they attain limited happiness and satisfaction from walking the right path. The more they persist in doing good deeds, which are also pleasant and good for them, the more they will attain good karma (good fate), by means of which they will merit a continued good life in this incarnation and also in the next. For the Buddhists too, like the Hindus, believe that life passes through countless incarnations. If a person chooses evil, he will be reincarnated into a difficult family, or even as an animal. Conversely, the better the path he walks, the more he will shape his karma in a better direction, and as a result he will be born in the next incarnation into a better life setting; until he reaches the high level attained by the monks who succeed in breaking free of the cycle of samsara (continuous motion) of reincarnation, and attain nirvana, which is eternal tranquillity.

More than half a billion people follow the ways of Buddhism. Admittedly, less than one percent of them follow the ways of the monks who disconnect completely from the life of this world; but many receive from Buddhism inspiration for a calm life, in which they feel satisfaction from the simple things of daily life, from refining their character traits and from doing good deeds, without expecting a reward other than the very satisfaction of being a good person. The way to achieve this is through various meditation exercises, in which a person practises observing the depths of his soul and gains strength to overcome his impulses.

In principle, Buddhism does not deal with God at all, but with paving the way to save man from his suffering and to guide him on a path that will give him tranquillity, enlightenment and satisfaction. Thus one can say that it is a religion without a god. This is why many people in the West find meaning in Buddhism, which gives them a path to a good and relaxed life without demanding that they believe in a higher power that oversees the world and commands how to behave.

However, since man is a believer by nature, Buddhists too need faith, and therefore the vast majority of them venerate statues in the image of Buddha, out of a belief that divine forces are revealed in him, and they believe that if they bring offerings before him or bow down to him, they will receive blessing. Therefore they are considered worshippers of avoda zara be-shituf, and all their rites are forbidden to Jews under the law of avoda zara (see Mareh Ha-bazak 6:61).

However, Buddhists who have risen above the idolatrous outlook and believe in a supreme source that is utterly beyond comprehension and does not reside in the statues are not considered worshippers of avoda zara at all. And even if they show respect to statues, this is not as worship but as an expression of respect for the idea and for the one who originated it.

sections.title: The Dharmic Religions
sections.html:
The Dharmic religions are the religions that originated in the Indian subcontinent. This family includes the Hindu religion and the three religions that grew out of it: Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism.

Jainism is an Indian religion that developed in the sixth century BCE, the same century in which Buddhism was founded. Jainism resembles Hinduism in that its adherents worship idol statues. According to Jainism every living creature has a spirit, and a person must respect the spirit in every living creature and refrain from harming it. Jain monks take extreme care not even to step on ants and insects. Believers in Jainism number between 4 and 12 million people, but their influence is great, because many of them belong to the affluent classes, and their moral principles have influenced many others. In general, Jainism can be defined as avoda zara be-shituf.

Sikhism is a religion founded some three hundred years ago in the Punjab region between India and Pakistan, and under the principle of belief in one God it incorporates Hindu, Muslim and other beliefs. The literal meaning of Sikhism is "followers of the way". The Sikhs number about 23 million people, and since they have no statues they are not considered worshippers of avoda zara.

sections.title: The Religions of China and Japan
sections.html:
On top of ancient idolatrous religions resembling the Hindu religion, two religions whose influence continues to this day were founded in the great kingdom of China some two thousand five hundred years ago: Confucianism and Daoism; and together with Buddhism, which came from India, these were the three main religions in China. Believers in Confucianism and Daoism continued to venerate idols and to practise ancestor worship, albeit in a more moderate form, because they emphasised wisdom over emotion and imagination. Following communism, which has ruled China for more than seventy years, the institutional framework of Confucianism and Daoism has passed from the world, though the legacy of their wisdom still influences Chinese culture.

Confucianism: founded by Confucius, who according to tradition was born in 551 BCE. His teaching lies on the border between religion and philosophy, and it educates its followers to be people of virtue: wise, believing, moral and broad-minded; loyal to tradition and to society, as a legacy of ancestor worship; loyal to the family and fulfilling their obligations, including that children honour and obey their parents, and the wife honours and obeys her parents and her husband. The loyalty also extends to other areas of life: a person respects his profession and is loyal to it, strives to learn it in the best possible way and to practise it in the most upright way. Every person must respect others according to their proper station, including the king his subjects and the subjects their king. There are still some two thousand temples of Confucius in Asia. Although there are statues in his image in the temples of Confucius, they do not worship him; rather, they burn incense and perform ceremonies as an expression of respect for the Confucian sages and of gratitude to the ancestors, without a cultic meaning, and consequently also without fixed and binding rules. Therefore one can say that there is no avoda zara in these temples.

Daoism: founded a little after Confucianism. Unlike Confucianism, which deals more with guiding action so as to reach the desired goal, Daoism deals more with the way, and with man's contact with the world of the spirit. The accepted translation of the word "Dao" is "the way", that is, the manner in which a person relates to his life and activity. At the core of Daoism is the understanding that the world is made up of opposites that complement one another, "yin" and "yang": cold and hot, slow and fast, darkness and light, woman and man. And the right way is for a person to combine the opposites in harmony, and not be drawn to one of the extremes. Out of this harmony one can rise to spiritual heights and attain eternal life. There are thousands of Daoist temples in Asia, with many idols and numerous detailed ceremonies, and therefore the temples, the idols and their worship are considered full-fledged avoda zara. However, it appears that most believers in Daoism believe in a supreme God, and therefore they are considered worshippers of avoda zara be-shituf.

Shinto: the folk religion of Japan, in which people believe in many idols that express forces of nature and ancient ancestors, venerate these idols and present offerings before them. There are many public Shinto shrines, most of them in small and modest buildings. In private homes, too, a small corner is dedicated to the gods. Many who visit Shinto shrines also visit Buddhist temples. Those who believe in idols alone sin with full-fledged avoda zara. And those who also include belief in a supreme God are considered worshippers of avoda zara be-shituf.
